extracted.intended_audience: press officers, science communicators, and public-relations professionals writing press releases about culturally contested science topics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for drafting press releases about scientifically contested, value-charged topics (e.g., climate, vaccines, AI safety) so they will be picked up and, crucially, received without identity-protective rejection. Emphasizes cultural-cognition research-informed techniques for message design and messenger selection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity-protective cognition
rubrics_metrics.description: Audiences accept evidence consistent with their cultural identity and reject evidence that threatens it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that recipients are motivated to preserve group-congruent beliefs; factual statements that appear to threaten group identity are likely to be dismissed regardless of evidence. Design releases with this cognitive dynamic in mind (see messenger selection, framing, pre-emption).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pollution of the science-communication environment
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a topic is 'polluted' by cultural-conflict cues, neutral information processing collapses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether prior public discourse has attached cultural-conflict cues to the topic (examples: climate, vaccines, GMO, gun violence, race-and-genetics, AI safety). If pollution is present, neutral or technocratic releases are likely to trigger polarized, identity-driven reactions rather than dispassionate evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusted-translator effect
rubrics_metrics.description: Acceptance depends on whether the messenger is culturally trusted by the recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selecting spokespeople who are trusted across relevant cultural groups — or providing multiple culturally-trusted messengers — amplifies the likelihood that the information will be accepted by diverse audiences. Messenger identity can matter more than technical credentials alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural framing of equivalent facts
rubrics_metrics.description: The same data, framed in technocratic / market / regulatory / individual-rights language, lands differently with different cultural worldviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide alternative framings of the same findings to align with different audience value-lens (e.g., market/individualism vs. regulatory/communitarian). Avoid assuming a single, neutral framing will be interpreted uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultural-pollution audit
rubrics_metrics.description: Has the topic been polluted by prior cultural-conflict framing (climate, vaccines, GMO, gun violence, race-and-genetics, AI safety)? If yes, generic release framing will trigger reactive rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before drafting, evaluate the public discourse history around the topic. If audit finds contamination, plan to use culturally-plural messengers, frame-pluralism, process emphasis, and other mitigation strategies rather than a single generic release.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diverse-messenger lineup
rubrics_metrics.description: Does the release name and quote scientists from multiple ideologically-coded backgrounds (e.g., a libertarian-trusted source and a communitarian-trusted source on the same finding)? The 'trusted translator' effect amplifies acceptance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intentionally include voices that signal credibility to different cultural groups. This can mean pairing scientists with differing public reputations or quoting trusted institutional figures across the spectrum to broaden acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame-pluralism
rubrics_metrics.description: Where possible, supply both a market/individualism-framed version and a regulatory/communitarian-framed version of the same release for differential distribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare multiple wording variants of the same core facts tailored to outlets serving distinct cultural cohorts. This improves pickup across ideologically-coded media and reduces identity-based dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of culturally-coded wedge language
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid lexical items that signal cultural alignment with one side ('climate denier', 'anti-vaxxer', 'gun nut', 'libtard'). These cues collapse the trust required for unbiased reception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edit copy to remove insult-laden or polarizing labels and moralizing epithets. Even accurate descriptors that function as identity cues can trigger rejection among the out-group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasis on process over conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: On contested topics, foregrounding scientific method (transparent data, pre-registration, replication) builds trust more than emphasizing the conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stress methodological transparency, replicability, data availability, and procedural safeguards in the release text rather than making strong normative or final-sounding claims. Process emphasis can reduce perceived threat to identity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-emption of motivated counter-reasoning
rubrics_metrics.description: Releases on contested topics should anticipate the most plausible identity-protective objection and address it factually within the release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the likely identity-protective counterarguments audiences may use and directly, neutrally address them (e.g., explain sample representativeness, limits, alternative interpretations) to reduce reactive dismissal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trusted-institution endorsement
rubrics_metrics.description: Quote endorsements from institutions trusted across the cultural spectrum (e.g., NAS, military, religious bodies) when appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible and appropriate, include institutional validation from entities that confer credibility across different cultural groups to enhance cross-cohort acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of moralized framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Kahan shows moralized framing reduces acceptance among the targeted out-group. Releases should report findings without moral verdicts on dissenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refrain from moral condemnation of those who disagree or from value-laden calls to virtue; keep tone descriptive and procedural rather than prescriptive or judgmental.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localized identity hooks
rubrics_metrics.description: Pickup increases when releases offer locally-relevant identity hooks (regional impacts, occupation-specific findings, community-led research).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor elements of the release to local identities (place, occupation, community) to increase relevance and uptake by outlets and audiences aligned with those identities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replication / consensus signal where genuine
rubrics_metrics.description: When a finding is part of an established scientific consensus, the release should mark that explicitly (e.g., 'This is consistent with the consensus view of [N] international assessments...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit consensus language and references only when empirically justified; false consensus claims undermine credibility. Signal replication and standing within the literature when accurate to strengthen acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pickup-worthiness implication for polluted vs. unpolluted topics
rubrics_metrics.description: On topics free of cultural pollution, traditional pickup criteria dominate (Sumner / Yavchitz / Schwitzer). On polluted topics, a pickup-worthy and effective release uses culturally-plural messengers, process-emphasis, and pre-emptive frame management.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply standard media pickup heuristics for neutral topics, but for polluted topics prioritize cultural-cognition strategies: supply differentiated frames for outlets serving specific cohorts (e.g., Fox, MSNBC, religious press), and craft multiple versions aligned to those audiences to maximize cross-spectrum pickup and actual persuasive impact.
